cards.b: Much of the universe is cold gas and dust that gives off almost no visible light. Radio and millimetre waves pass through that dust, so radio telescopes can see the birth of stars and planets that optical telescopes miss. Dust that blocks visible light is largely transparent at radio wavelengths, so radio can see through the clouds where stars form.

cards.h: Karl Jansky and the first radio sky
cards.b: In 1932 the engineer Karl Jansky, working for Bell Labs, detected radio waves coming from the Milky Way. This was the start of radio astronomy. Grote Reber later built a dish in his Illinois backyard in 1937 and mapped the radio sky himself. Jansky built his antenna to study static on transatlantic radio links, and that is how he noticed cosmic noise.

cards.h: Why a dish is not enough
cards.b: A single dish has poor resolution at long wavelengths. Interferometry links many dishes so that together they act like one giant telescope. Resolution depends on the largest distance between dishes, called the baseline, not on the dish size alone. At one millimetre wavelength, a 1-kilometre baseline would resolve about 0.2 arcseconds, far sharper than any single small dish.

The Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array sits on the Chajnantor plateau in Chile, at about 5,000 metres. It has 66 antennas. Its longest baselines are around 16 kilometres. The thin, dry air there absorbs much of the water vapour that blocks millimetre waves.

In 2014 ALMA imaged the young star HL Tauri. The image showed rings and gaps in its dust disc. These gaps are thought to be where young planets are clearing their paths. This was one of the clearest views yet of planet formation. The disc around HL Tauri is only about a million years old, which is very young by stellar standards.

Electrons spiralling in magnetic fields give off synchrotron radiation, a smooth radio glow. Supernova remnants and jets from black holes shine this way. Radio maps therefore show where magnetic fields and fast particles are, which light often hides. Radio maps of synchrotron glow are used to measure magnetic field strengths in distant galaxies.

ALMA images are not taken like photographs. Each antenna measures signals, and computers combine the signals from every pair of dishes. Astronomers check the results against known objects and against other observatories, which is how radio images are trusted. Interferometric images are cleaned with computer algorithms, so astronomers always publish their method and error limits.

• 'Radio telescopes take photos like cameras.' They measure waves, and images are computed.
  • 'Radio waves are only for communication.' Most radio waves here come from the cosmos.
  • 'One big dish always sees best.' Linked arrays can resolve finer detail.
Radio dishes also do not stare at one point; they track objects as Earth turns.

The Ooty Radio Telescope in Tamil Nadu, built in 1970 by the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, is a long cylindrical dish of about 530 metres. The Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope near Pune, run by the National Centre for Radio Astrophysics, uses 30 steerable dishes of 45 metres each.

• Radio waves pass through cold dust that blocks light.
  • Karl Jansky detected the Milky Way in radio in 1932.
  • Interferometry links dishes into one large telescope.
  • ALMA in Chile images planet-forming discs.

Think about it: (1) Why must ALMA sit at high altitude? (2) Why do linked dishes beat a single dish of the same total area?
